info.description:
## Persistent Cognitive Memory for AI Agents

Write memories, query with semantic + episodic search, learn from outcomes via valence,
and compress with sleep consolidation.

### Quick Start
- `POST /api/v1/memory/write` -- store an insight
- `POST /api/v1/memory/read` -- recall relevant memories
- `POST /api/v1/memory/feedback` -- teach the system what worked
- `POST /api/v1/memory/consolidate` -- compress similar memories
- `GET /api/v1/memory/stats` -- see memory state
- `WS /api/v1/memory/stream` -- real-time updates (WebSocket)

post.description:
Store a new memory atom.

Content is embedded, filtered by importance, then stored with Hebbian links.

With `supersedes`, the write instead replaces the listed atoms: the successor
is stored and every target is marked as superseded by it, in one transaction
— all of it or none of it. The importance/novelty REJECTION is skipped for
such a write (a successor resembles its predecessor by construction) while
the score is still computed and returned.

Store multiple memory atoms in one request. Each atom is processed sequentially.

`supersedes` is refused here (422) — see `_reject_supersedes_in_batch`.

Query memory.

Episodic exact match (if fingerprint), then semantic search and Hebbian expansion.

Bounded read of the concept-association graph around `seeds` (core#630).

Distinct from `/memory/read`'s `expanded_concepts` (names only, discarded
weights): this returns the actual `hebbian_edges` rows — weight, valence,
count — for a caller-supplied neighbourhood, never the whole org's graph
(`PostgresStorage.load_hebbian_edges` stays reserved for the single-tenant
WS viz snapshot it was built for). Same org resolution and auth/scope as
`/memory/read` — a read-only op, `require_write=False`.

An unknown seed (or one whose edges all fall below `min_weight`) simply
contributes nothing: an all-unknown `seeds` list is a 200 empty graph, not
a 404 — same "absence is not an error" contract as `/memory/recent`.

`req.domain` reaches `_resolve_target_org` exactly like `/memory/read`'s
does: an `xroom:<room_id>` value resolves to that room's OWN storage
bucket (after the membership/scope check) — a real change of which org's
edges get read, not a filter within one org. Any other value is inert
(`hebbian_edges` has no `domain` column), same as passing none.

Queryless newest-first feed (#404 R5) — backs MCP ``memory_list_recent``.

A keyset walk over ``(created_at DESC, id DESC)``, complete by
construction: the temporal complement of /memory/read's semantic gate.
An empty feed is ``200 {"items": [], "next_cursor": null}`` and NEVER a
404 — the shipped MCP client reads a bare 404 as "endpoint not deployed"
and hides the feature behind a fallback hint.
Report outcome for atoms (success/failure). Updates valence and Hebbian weights.
Run soft consolidation behind the explicit single-worker safety gate.

has JOINED, each with its ready-to-use ``xroom:<room_id>`` address and the caller's
role — so a fresh agent session can RE-FIND its rooms instead of only being able to

post.description:
Create a room owned by the AUTHENTICATED account (Rooms Wave 2).

Unlike the portal-plane ``/rooms`` routes (which require ``X-Admin-Key`` + a
verified session), this endpoint lives on the tenant ``router`` and derives
the owner from ``request.state.claims`` — the org that the auth middleware
(DB-backed ``mk_live_`` key / JWT) populated. So an agent holding only its
``mk_live_`` key can provision its own room. The owner is taken from the
key's claims (``_get_org_id``), NEVER the request body (the schema also
forbids a body-supplied ``owner_org_id``) — the same anti-self-grant
invariant the portal path enforces from the session.

Note: this path is NOT in the middleware's portal-prefix bypass list
(``/admin``/``/rooms``/``/projects``), so tenant-key auth runs here as normal.
A fresh room seeds its owner as a ``read_write`` member (see
``RoomStore.create_room``), so the owner can immediately read/write it via
the ``xroom:<room_id>`` address; inviting OTHER accounts is a separate step.

delete.description: Wipe all atoms, links, fingerprints. Requires ALLOW_RESET=true.

Delete a single atom by ID. Hebbian edges are left untouched.

Deleting an atom removes that atom's row and nothing else. In
particular it does NOT sweep Hebbian edges: `hebbian_edges` has no
foreign key to `atoms` (endpoints are plain concept strings), so no
edge dangles when an atom dies, and the associations learned from
retrieval (`co_activate`) are cross-atom by construction — they are
not derivable from any single atom's `concepts` list. The
post-delete sweep that used to run here deleted exactly those
learned edges and kept only the redundant, atom-derivable ones; it
was removed 2026-08-20. See ADR-012 errata.

Secret-atoms (the caller's Vault) are immutable via this endpoint
(Design 13): `storage.delete_atoms` silently skips them, so a 0-row
delete is disambiguated below — a real secret-atom returns 403
instead of the ordinary idempotent `{"deleted": 0}`.

**Deleting an atom that sits in a supersession chain is permitted and
LOUD.** Delete is administrative and destructive by design, and refusing
it would leave a tenant unable to remove their own data — so instead the
response says what it broke: `superseded_predecessors_left_hidden` names
the atoms that are now marked superseded with nothing pointing at them —
permanently so, once read-side filtering (D2) makes that marking hide them —
and `history_destroyed` says the revision chain lost a link.

get.description: Point read: retrieve full atom detail by ID (for debug/tracing).

delete.description:
Delete all atoms in a domain. Hebbian edges are left untouched.

Tenant-scoped: only deletes atoms in the calling org's scope.
Hebbian edges are not swept — see `delete_atom` above for why there
is no such thing as an orphan edge here. Wiping one domain therefore
leaves every association learned over other domains' atoms intact.

Secret-atoms (the caller's Vault) are immutable via this endpoint
(Design 13): they are filtered out before delete, never wiped, and
the count excluded is reported as `skipped_secrets`.

Like `delete_atom`, a wipe that breaks supersession chains says so — as
`superseded_predecessors_left_hidden_count` (an int; `delete_atom` returns
the ids themselves, hence the different name for the different shape),
because a domain can hold arbitrarily many. A predecessor living INSIDE the
wiped domain is deleted alongside its successor and is therefore not "left
hidden"; only predecessors in other domains are.

Liveness probe: is the process alive? Fast, no DB check.
Readiness probe: is the service ready to serve traffic? Checks engine + DB.

Deep readiness check.

``ready`` = database AND engine (the hard dependencies) → HTTP 503 when
false, so an orchestrator healthcheck (Railway) refuses to promote a build
whose startup failed (FAILURE-SURFACE P0-4: the old contract was HTTP 200
with ``ready: false`` in the body, which promoted broken builds).

``checks.warm`` is reported to every caller: True when the warm-up is
disabled, its readiness gate
(`Settings.concept_expander_warm_ready_gate_seconds`, 0 = off by default)
is 0, THIS process's warm run has finished, or the gate's time cap has
elapsed. It turns ``ready`` false, and the answer into a 503, ONLY for the
orchestrator's deploy healthcheck (`_is_deploy_healthcheck`: Railway
probes from `healthcheck.railway.app`, at the start of a deployment only),
because holding traffic promotion is the gate's one purpose. A process
restarted after a crash takes traffic with no healthcheck at all, so every
other reader is asking about a process that is already serving and gets
``ready: true`` with ``checks.warm: false``. The wait is bounded by the cap
in every case, including a warm run that never starts. See
`_resolve_warm_check`.

``checks.embedding`` is a LIVE vendor call (cached 60 s — see
``_probe_embedding``). It does NOT gate ``ready``: a dead embedding vendor
yields HTTP 200 with ``degraded: true`` so the fix for a vendor outage can
still be deployed *during* the outage, and external probes alert on
``degraded`` instead. Probes must assert ``ready && !degraded``.

503.description: Not ready: database or engine is down, or the (bounded) concept-expander warm-up gate has not yet opened (same body, `ready: false`).

post.description:
Batch write up to 100 memory atoms.

## Idempotency

Supports the Stripe-style `Idempotency-Key` header. Clients that retry
the same logical write after a network failure (including the 2026-04-13
Cloudflare 524 / ghost-write scenario) can pass the same key and get
back the exact response the server cached on the first successful
processing, rather than double-writing atoms. The cache TTL is 24 hours
(see migrations/versions/004_idempotency.py).

The key is scoped per operation and per organization by
`_scoped_idempotency_key` so two tenants cannot collide on the same
raw UUID. The org fragment is a SHA-256 hash prefix, not the raw
org_id, to make the key delimiter-safe regardless of what characters
the upstream auth layer produces.

### ⚠️ Sequential retries only

This implementation protects **sequential** retries (client waits for
the first request to return or time out, then retries with the same
key). **Concurrent** retries are NOT serialized: if two retries of
the same key land while the first processing is still in flight,
both will observe a cache miss and both will call `engine.write()`.
In practice MCP clients retry with exponential backoff so this race
is rare, but if the dashboards surface it as a real signal we will
add a processing-sentinel row inserted with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`
at the top of the handler (tracked as Step 2c.1 in the observability
sprint plan). Documented so a future reader does not assume the
current code is fully race-safe.

### Failure modes

* Missing or empty header → no caching, behaves as before.
* Header > 240 chars → 400 VALIDATION_ERROR (table column is 255).
* Cache lookup DB error → falls through to normal processing (we
  prefer a duplicate write over a hard failure on the retry path).
* Cache store DB error → the response is still returned to the
  client; we log the cache failure and move on so the successful
  write is not lost.
Batch read up to 50 queries.
Advanced query: multi-domain, metadata filters, same response shape as /memory/read.

get.description:
Every revision reachable from this one by supersession links.

`include_history` on a read grants ELIGIBILITY: history competes under the
same ranking, `min_relevance` and `top_k` as everything else, so a read can
legitimately return part of a chain and no read can promise all of it. This
endpoint is the handle that does promise all of it — hand it any revision,
get the whole chain.

The walk goes BOTH ways: up through `superseded_by` to the live tip, and
down through `supersedes` — which is a LIST, because one successor may
consolidate several predecessors (D3 §1), so starting from one consumed
revision still reveals its siblings.

It hydrates through `get_atom`, the point read, which resolves any revision
regardless of the read-side filter (contract §7). A chain is therefore
available whether or not that filter is enabled: it is a fact about the
data, not a behaviour of the filter.

Revisions come back in topological order — a predecessor never follows
something that replaced it — with `created_at` deciding only between
branches the links leave unordered. See `_chain_order`; ordering by time
alone is wrong on any host whose clock is coarser than its write rate.

Failure modes are answers, not errors. A pointer that resolves to nothing —
the successor was destroyed by the loud delete handle (#518), or belongs to
another tenant — is reported in `dangling`; running out of point-read budget
sets `truncated`. That budget counts every resolution, missed ones included,
so `revisions` can stop short of `CHAIN_MAX_NODES` when the chain is full of
holes — `truncated` is the signal, never the length. An unknown or foreign
starting id is a 404, indistinguishable from each other by design (the same
anti-oracle rule the plain GET follows).

get.description:
Stream all memories for the calling org as JSONL.

Universal data portability: every user can take their memories with
them at any time, in every subscription state. Used to fulfill the
refund-policy promise that downgraded users have 30 days to export
before atom-limit grace expires.

- Auth: standard tenant API key (X-Api-Key)
- Format: newline-delimited JSON, one atom per line
- Streaming: server-side cursor, no in-memory buffering — works for
  Free (10K) through Team (5M) without OOM
- Embeddings excluded (large, model-specific, derivable from content)

Reads NEVER blocked guarantee applies — export works in active,
past_due, over_limit, suspended states.

Discovery: list the caller's secrets as VALUE-FREE metadata (alias, context,
created_at, concepts) so an agent can FIND a secret by alias WITHOUT ever seeing a
value. The tenant comes from the VERIFIED claims and scopes the query (org A can
never enumerate org B's secrets). A secret-atom with no reachable ``secret:{alias}``
external_ref (e.g. stored directly, not via this route) is SKIPPED — its alias could
not be used via the by-alias route anyway, so surfacing it would only mislead.

post.description:
Mint a key into the authenticated user's OWN user_<sub> tenant. Two proofs: X-Admin-Key
(caller = portal, via _require_admin) AND a valid forwarded user session (via _verify_session_sub).
The org is DERIVED from the session, never from the body — so this path may target the reserved
user_ namespace that POST /admin/keys forbids, without weakening that guard.

Get-or-create the per-user API key the remote MCP server (RS) uses to call
core on behalf of a connector user. TWO proofs (like ``/keys/self-serve``): the
``X-Admin-Key`` (caller = the trusted RS) AND the user's OIDC access token
forwarded as ``X-Connector-Token`` (verified against the AS JWKS). The org is
DERIVED from the verified ``sub`` (``user_<sub>``), never from the body — so this
path may target the reserved ``user_`` namespace WITHOUT weakening the
``POST /admin/keys`` guard.

Revokes any prior active connector key for this (user, client_label) and mints a
fresh one (the raw key is only knowable at creation; the RS caches it). Invariant:
at most one ACTIVE connector key per (user, client_label) — different clients
(claude, chatgpt, ...) hold their own keys simultaneously; the NULL group (older
RS builds) is matched via IS NOT DISTINCT FROM. All keys are tagged
``name="__connector__"`` so they never collide with the user's own portal keys.

Tier and limits come from the ORG SUBSCRIPTION, not the body: enforcement
(``DailyQuotaMiddleware`` in ``usage.py``) reads limits from the KEY row, so
connector traffic must carry the org plan rather than hardcoded free defaults.
Keys rotate hourly, so later plan changes self-heal within an hour. The body's
tier/limit fields are IGNORED (wire compat with older RS builds only).

delete.description:
Cascade-delete every resource belonging to a single tenant.

Closes Issue #265: until this endpoint existed, the only way to undo a
bench / demo / QA / preview run was per-domain ``DELETE
/memory/domain/{domain}`` calls, which left orphan Hebbian edges,
fingerprints, and api_keys behind — exactly the asymmetry that let the
overnight benchmark loop dump ~200 atoms into the founder's prod org
with no clean recovery path.

What gets deleted (single atomic transaction in
``PostgresStorage.cascade_delete_org``):

1. atoms — every row WHERE ``organization_id = $1``
2. hebbian_edges — every row WHERE ``organization_id = $1``
   (by-org direct DELETE, not orphan-cleanup: atomic transaction
   means no concurrent INSERT into atoms can re-create a
   supporting row mid-cascade)
3. episodic_fingerprints — whole tenant slice WHERE ``organization_id = $1``
4. api_keys — soft-delete (``UPDATE is_active=FALSE``) so the audit
   trail (created_at / last_used_at / tier history) survives for
   compliance. Hard-delete is the wrong default — it loses
   billing-relevant provenance and any post-mortem signal about
   who used what.
5. org_subscriptions — the billing row (Stripe ids + contact-email
   PII), so a recreated org doesn't inherit a stale tier and no
   orphaned PII is left behind.
6. usage_daily — the per-org usage history.

After the transaction commits, the subscription cache is invalidated and the
org's in-memory per-org engine state (Hebbian graph, concept index, episodic
fingerprints) is evicted, so a recreated org reusing the same id starts truly
clean — no "ghost-tenant" via cached tier or in-memory slots.

Guards (defense-in-depth):

* ``_require_admin`` — X-Admin-Key matches ADMIN_API_KEY setting.
  Constant-time compare via ``secrets.compare_digest``.
* ``_validate_deletable_org`` — rejects the reserved ``user_`` OIDC
  namespace so a leaked ADMIN_API_KEY cannot wipe a real user's tenant,
  while still allowing ``room_``/``proj_`` bucket cleanup (the mint guard,
  by contrast, rejects ALL system prefixes).
* default-sentinel guard — also refuses ``settings.default_org`` so a
  fat-finger cannot TRUNCATE a whole single-tenant deployment.
* Storage runs inside ``_scoped(organization_id)`` which opens a
  single ``conn.transaction()`` and sets the tenant GUC so
  Postgres RLS (migration 013) authorises every statement under
  the non-superuser ``mnemo_app`` role; the explicit
  ``WHERE organization_id = $1`` clauses are the second layer.

Idempotency: a second call against the same ``org_id`` returns all-zero
counts ``{atoms, hebbian_edges, fingerprints, keys_revoked,
org_subscriptions, usage_daily, org_settings, org_settings_audit}`` — every
delete is a no-op once the tenant is empty. Safe to retry on transport
failure.

Returns: ``{organization_id, deleted: {atoms, hebbian_edges, fingerprints,
keys_revoked, org_subscriptions, usage_daily, org_settings,
org_settings_audit}}``.

Raises:
    HTTPException(400): organization_id has user_ prefix or invalid shape.
    HTTPException(401): X-Admin-Key missing or wrong.
    HTTPException(503): admin key not configured or DB pool unavailable.

get.description: Get daily usage for an organization (last N days).

Platform-wide usage aggregated across ALL organizations for the
last N days (default 7).

Powers the portal admin dashboard's "platform usage" card. v1 is
operational-only: reads/writes/feedbacks/queries, distinct active
keys, distinct organizations, and the top 10 orgs by query volume.

Response notes for consumers: the top-level totals cover ALL
organizations, whereas `top_orgs_by_queries` is only the TOP 10 — do
NOT sum it to derive the platform total (use `total_queries`). The
`daily` array is ordered newest-first by date and omits days with no
activity (gaps mean zero), so its length may be < `days`.

`days` is validated to `[1, 90]` at the FastAPI layer via `Query`
(HTTP 422 before any DB work). The window itself is computed in
Postgres as `CURRENT_DATE - make_interval(days => $1)` with the day
count bound as a parameter — never string-interpolated. The only
interpolated token in any of these queries is `{schema}`, which is a
validated SQL identifier from settings (`validate_sql_identifier`),
not request input.

Live account-level aggregates over personal (``user_``) orgs.

Mirrors the portal sweep's definitions so a live tile and last night's
rollup describe the same population:

* ``orgs_with_atoms`` / ``atoms_total`` — accounts holding at least one
  memory, and the platform total (sweep: ``atoms > 0`` / ``SUM(atoms)``).
  These two are read through the storage layer's maintenance route, NOT
  this handler's pool: ``atoms`` is under FORCE RLS (013) plus 027's
  RESTRICTIVE room policies, and a pooled count with no tenant context
  answers a silent zero — which is precisely what this endpoint shipped to
  the console on 2026-08-10. They are NULL, with a reason, whenever that
  route cannot answer. The default-off ``ADMIN_ATOMS_AGGREGATES_ENABLED``
  kill switch also returns NULL without calling storage; neither path ever
  produces a fallback zero.
* ``orgs_with_active_key`` — accounts with a live key (``active_keys > 0``).
* ``orgs_called_30d`` — accounts with any read or write inside the
  window; feedbacks deliberately NOT counted, matching the sweep's
  ``reads_30d + writes_30d > 0``.
* ``paying_org_ids`` — non-free tiers as a list (see block comment: the
  grant carve-out is the portal's to apply). ``status`` is deliberately
  not filtered — the sweep's per-org read doesn't filter it either, and
  the two surfaces must not disagree about who counts.

``days`` is bound as a SQL parameter; the only interpolated token is the
validated ``{schema}`` identifier — same guarantees as
``aggregate/usage`` above.

put.description: Set or clear the per-org LLM provider override.

Set or clear the per-org embedding-model pin.

Mirrors ``set_org_llm_provider``: an ``UPDATE org_subscriptions ... RETURNING``
+ invalidation of the engine's in-memory per-org embedding cache so the pin
takes effect for the very next request ON THIS WORKER (other workers pick it
up after their next restart — same accepted multi-worker tradeoff as the LLM
pref cache).

🔴 ADR-021 M2 — per-org embedding dispatch (M1.5) + coexisting-dimension storage
(M2) are LIVE. The engine resolves the org's OWN ``EmbeddingService`` per request
(``_resolve_org_embedding_service``), and M2 added the per-dim storage columns
(``_EMBEDDING_DIM_COLUMNS`` — the SSOT for which dims are storeable). A pin is
effective once its produced vector has a column to land in — ``effective =
(pin.dim == global.dim) OR (a routing column exists for pin.dim)``:
  * same-dim pin → ``effective=true`` (existing atoms migrate via
    ``scripts/reembed_atoms.py``; no re-embed needed for new writes);
  * STOREABLE cross-dim pin (e.g. text-embedding-3-small@1536 after migration 022
    added ``embedding_1536``) → ``effective=true`` — new vectors land in the
    matching per-dim column, cross-dim isolated from the global corpus;
  * UNSTOREABLE cross-dim pin (a dim with no routing column yet, e.g. 3072) →
    ``effective=false`` — recorded as the re-embed target once a column is added.
We RECORD the pin either way (so an operator-driven re-embed has its target).
Returning the row (record) is more useful than a hard 409 (reject): the pin is
the persisted target the dispatch + re-embed read.

🔴 Cache-race serialization (MUST-FIX): the DB UPDATE and the in-memory cache
mutation are held under a per-org ``asyncio.Lock`` so a concurrent PUT for the
SAME org cannot interleave between commit and cache-update and leave the cache
reflecting the losing write.

get.description:
The organisation's per-org flags: the stored override (null = unset),
the resolved effective value, and which tier of the resolution order
decided it. ``history`` is the last twenty audit rows, newest first.

``effective`` describes enforced behaviour, not intent. ``effective.
supersede_read_filter`` is what the storage read gate applies;
``effective.auto_consolidation`` is what the engine's write-triggered
consolidation applies - both trigger sites in ``MemoryEngine._write_inner``
resolve it through ``_peeked_auto_consolidation``, the same pure function
this response uses, so a row saying ``false`` suppresses the pass while the
fleet flag is on rather than merely being reported here. (Admin-triggered
consolidation is an explicit operator action and is out of its scope.)
Writing ``auto_consolidation: true`` is still refused by the PUT until
phase 4, so a row can only narrow the fleet default today.

The row and its history are read in ONE transaction
(``get_org_settings_with_history``), so the two halves of this response are
one snapshot: a PUT landing mid-request cannot produce ``settings`` from
before the change beside a ``history`` that already lists it.

A ``room_*`` bucket is refused with a typed 400 - see
``_refuse_room_bucket``; a malformed or oversize id with a typed 400 -
see ``_validate_settings_org``.

put.description:
Set (or clear, with an explicit ``null``) either per-org flag.

Idempotent: a request that changes nothing returns ``changed: []`` and
writes no audit row - enforced by ``storage.upsert_org_settings`` itself;
this route only decides WHICH keys count as "the caller asked to change
this" (``model_fields_set``) before handing them down, and invalidates
the resolver's cached entry for this organisation after a real change so
the very next request on this worker sees it. A change to
``supersede_read_filter`` additionally drops this organisation's concept
index (``engine.drop_org_concept_index``), which the resolver
invalidation alone would leave at the pre-flip filter state permanently.

Propagation: the change is live immediately on THIS instance, and within
``ORG_SETTINGS_TTL_SECONDS`` (default 60 s) on every other API instance -
invalidation is per-worker, and other workers converge when their cached
entry expires (core#601 decision R6). There is no fleet-wide invalidation
and none is needed at this TTL. The concept index converges on the same
schedule: each worker's next flags refresh compares the resolved value
against the one its index was built under and drops it on a difference
(``MemoryEngine._note_supersede_state``).

get.description: Get memory statistics for a specific organization.

Get recent memories for a specific organization.

Direct storage path — does NOT go through `engine.read()` or the
retrieval pipeline. Previously this endpoint built a
`ReadRequest(query="*", top_k=50)` and ran the whole classify +
IRCOT + concept-expansion stack just to surface 10 recent rows
for the admin dashboard. That was the only admin endpoint
transiting the retrieval engine, and under pool starvation it
became the dominant blast-radius source for the 2026-04-13
incident (Issue #112).

The refactored path calls `storage.get_recent_atoms(org_id, limit)`
directly — a single indexed SELECT with P0.1's pool-timeout
protection. Response time drops from seconds (or minutes on a
starved pool) to single-digit milliseconds.

`limit` is validated to `[1, 50]` at the FastAPI layer via `Query`.
Previously `limit` was a bare `int = 10` with only a runtime
`min(limit, 50)` clamp — a client sending `limit=0` or `limit=-1`
would reach Postgres with `LIMIT -1`, which the server treats as
"no limit" on some versions and as a query error on others. Either
way a misleading response (or a pool-held slow query on a large
tenant). `Query(ge=1, le=50)` rejects the out-of-range value as
HTTP 422 before any DB work happens.

atom_id.title: Atom Id
atom_id.description: The revision the walk started from.

revisions.title: Revisions
revisions.description: Every revision found, roots to head. Ordered topologically along the supersedes links — a predecessor never follows something that replaced it; creation time decides only between branches the links leave genuinely unordered (e.g. two predecessors consolidated by one successor).

dangling.title: Dangling
dangling.description: Chain pointers that resolved to nothing — the referenced revision was destroyed by the loud delete handle, or belongs to another tenant. Reported as breaks in the chain rather than raised: the caller already holds these ids, they came off rows the caller can read.

truncated.title: Truncated
truncated.description: True when the walk exhausted its lookup budget and stopped early, so `revisions` is a prefix of the chain rather than all of it. The budget counts EVERY lookup — resolved revisions and dangling-pointer misses alike — so a heavily-damaged chain can set this with far fewer than 64 revisions returned; do not infer chain length from it. A cap that truncated silently would let a caller believe they hold the whole history.

AtomChainSchema.title: AtomChainSchema
AtomChainSchema.description:

`include_history` grants ELIGIBILITY under ranking — it never promised a
complete chain, and the read schemas say so. This is the handle that does
promise one. It hydrates through the point read, which resolves any
revision regardless of the read-side filter, so a chain is available whether
or not that filter is enabled: it is a fact about the data.

GraphEdgeSchema.title: GraphEdgeSchema
GraphEdgeSchema.description:
One association edge, as stored in `mnemo.hebbian_edges`.

Undirected by construction: `sync_hebbian_edges` persists exactly one row
per unordered concept pair (`hebbian.py` dedupes on `(min(a,b), max(a,b))`
before flush), so `source`/`target` reflect storage order, not the order
concepts were learned in. core#630's open question ("directed pairs or
collapsed to one undirected edge per pair?") is answered by this existing
invariant — there is only ever one row per pair to report.

degree.title: Degree
degree.description: Number of returned edges touching this concept — a property of THIS response's edge set, not the concept's total degree across the org's whole graph (which `limit`/`truncated` may cut short).

GraphNodeSchema.title: GraphNodeSchema
GraphNodeSchema.description: One concept in the returned association graph.

seeds.title: Seeds
seeds.description: Concept names to center the graph on. 1-20 items, each at most 200 characters (the `VARCHAR(200)` width of hebbian_edges.source_concept/target_concept — a longer string can never match a stored concept).

depth.title: Depth
depth.description: Hop count from the seeds. depth=1 returns only edges touching a seed directly; depth=2/3 walk further, one hop per level. Each hop is independently bounded server-side by a per-hop row cap (see `truncated`). When `min_weight` is null AND this REQUESTED depth is >= 2, EVERY hop of the walk — including the first, hop 0 — floors the edge weight at 0.05 (reported back as `min_weight_applied`), so an unfiltered multi-hop walk from a hub concept cannot fan out across an org's whole graph before `limit` ever applies, and a depth=2 request cannot return a direct seed edge the floor would otherwise have excluded one hop later. An EXPLICIT `min_weight` (including `0.0`) is honoured at every hop instead, with no server override.

domain.title: Domain
domain.description: Same mechanism as /memory/read, not a filter over one org's edges: an `xroom:<room_id>` value resolves (after the membership/scope check) to that ROOM's own storage bucket, so the graph is read from the room's `hebbian_edges` rows instead of the caller's own — this is NOT inert. Any other value (or null) IS inert: `hebbian_edges` has no `domain` column, so a plain domain string does not narrow which edges/atoms count — it has the same effect as omitting the field entirely.

min_weight.title: Min Weight
min_weight.description: Drop edges below this weight. null = no caller-supplied floor at depth 1; when the REQUESTED depth is >= 2, the server applies its own floor (0.05, see `depth`) at every hop of the walk, including hop 0 — reported back as `min_weight_applied`. An EXPLICIT value (including `0.0`) is honoured at EVERY hop with no server override, so `min_weight=0.0` at depth>=2 really does return every edge down to weight 0.

limit.title: Limit
limit.description: Maximum number of edges to return. Mirrors ReadRequestSchema.top_k's bounds.

New endpoint, no back-compat surface yet, so `extra="forbid"` rejects an
unknown field outright rather than silently dropping it (unlike
`ReadRequestSchema`, which predates that convention and cannot adopt it
now without breaking older clients — see the note on `include_history`).

nodes.title: Nodes
nodes.description: Concepts touched by `edges` below. A seed with no surviving edge (unknown concept, or every edge fell below `min_weight`) is NOT listed — nodes are derived from the returned edges, not echoed from the request.

truncated.title: Truncated
truncated.description: True when either a per-hop server-side cap or the request's `limit` cut the walk short — the graph may hold more edges than are reported here.

min_weight_applied.title: Min Weight Applied
min_weight_applied.description: The weight floor actually used at EVERY hop of the walk. Equal to the request's `min_weight` when it was set (an explicit value, including `0.0`, is never overridden); equal to the server floor 0.05 when the request left `min_weight` null and the REQUESTED `depth` was >= 2 (applied from hop 0 onward, not just hop 1 onward); equal to `0.0` when it was null and `depth == 1`.

(``MemoryEngine._supersede_read_filter_on`` / ``_peeked_supersede``).

``auto_consolidation`` is the value the engine's write-triggered
consolidation pass applies (``MemoryEngine._peeked_auto_consolidation``,
consulted at both ``_write_inner`` trigger sites): every

include_history.title: Include History
include_history.description: Return superseded revisions alongside live ones; each carries `superseded_by`, and every item carries `supersedes` when it replaced something. ReadyResponseSchema.title: ReadyResponseSchema
ReadyResponseSchema.description:
Deep readiness check (DB + engine + concept-expander warm-up + embedding vendor).

Two verdicts, deliberately separate (FAILURE-SURFACE 2026-08-26, P0-3/P0-4):

* ``ready`` - the hard dependencies (database, engine). ``false`` is served
  as **HTTP 503**, so an orchestrator healthcheck refuses to promote a build
  whose startup failed. For the orchestrator's deploy healthcheck ONLY, a
  warm-up still inside its gate also makes ``ready`` false (see below).
* ``degraded`` — ``ready`` but the LIVE embedding probe failed. Served as
  **HTTP 200**, so a vendor outage never blocks deploying its own fix.
  External probes must assert ``ready == true && degraded == false``.

``checks.embedding`` is a real vendor call (cached 60 s server-side, probe
text time-bucketed to defeat the embedding LRU), not a wiring check.

``checks.warm`` is reported to every caller and is bounded: with the
warm-up enabled and its readiness gate
(`CONCEPT_EXPANDER_WARM_READY_GATE_SECONDS`, max 200) set positive, it is
false while the current process's warm run is still inside the window. It
makes ``ready`` false (HTTP 503) only for a probe whose `Host` is
`CONCEPT_EXPANDER_WARM_READY_GATE_HOST` (default
`healthcheck.railway.app`, Railway's deploy healthcheck), so that traffic
promotion waits for the warm-up. Every other caller keeps getting
``ready: true``: after a crash restart the process serves traffic at once,
and reporting it as not ready would report an outage that is not
happening. Never longer than the cap, and never at all with the gate
at its default of 0 or the warm-up disabled.
